clinicalPearls: Develops when long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism, usually from chronic kidney disease, progresses to autonomous PTH secretion that persists despite correction of the original stimulus
Characterised biochemically by hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately high PTH, in contrast to the hypocalcaemia or normocalcaemia of secondary disease
Classically emerges after successful renal transplantation, when the previously enlarged, autonomous glands continue to oversecrete despite restored renal function
Chronically stimulated glands undergo nodular hyperplasia with reduced calcium-sensing receptor and vitamin D receptor expression, driving the shift to autonomy
Persistent hypercalcaemia threatens the transplanted kidney and accelerates vascular and soft-tissue calcification and bone disease
Medical therapy with calcimimetics can lower calcium and PTH, but truly autonomous, refractory disease often requires parathyroidectomy
Surgical options include subtotal parathyroidectomy or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation, balancing recurrence against the risk of permanent hypoparathyroidism
reference.pathophysiology: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism represents the transition of chronically stimulated parathyroid glands to autonomous hormone secretion. In chronic kidney disease, persistent hyperphosphataemia, reduced active vitamin D, and hypocalcaemia drive secondary hyperparathyroidism with diffuse then nodular parathyroid hyperplasia. Over years, nodular areas develop monoclonal expansion with down-regulation of the calcium-sensing and vitamin D receptors, so the glands no longer respond appropriately to normalised calcium and continue to oversecrete PTH. When the underlying stimulus is removed, most notably after renal transplantation, this autonomous secretion produces frank hypercalcaemia and ongoing skeletal and vascular injury.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic kidney disease
Immobilisation or vitamin D-related hypercalcaemia in renal patients
Aluminium or adynamic bone disease affecting calcium handling
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate, and intact PTH demonstrating hypercalcaemia with inappropriately high PTH
Assessment of renal function and transplant status
Vitamin D status and markers of bone turnover
Neck ultrasound and sestamibi or 4D-CT to assess gland number and enlargement before surgery
Bone density and skeletal imaging for renal osteodystrophy and fractures
Imaging for vascular and soft-tissue calcification when clinically indicated
redFlags: Progressive hypercalcaemia threatening a transplanted kidney
Calciphylaxis or extensive vascular and soft-tissue calcification
Severe bone disease with pathological fractures
Symptomatic hypercalcaemic crisis requiring urgent treatment
reference.prognosis: Autonomous glands may occasionally regress after transplantation, but persistent tertiary disease generally requires calcimimetics or parathyroidectomy; surgery is usually curative, with the main trade-off being recurrence versus permanent hypoparathyroidism.
pitfalls: Confusing tertiary disease with primary hyperparathyroidism and overlooking the underlying renal history
Persisting with medical therapy alone in truly autonomous, refractory disease that warrants surgery
Failing to monitor calcium after transplantation and missing evolving autonomy
Underestimating the risk of profound postoperative hypocalcaemia and hungry bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Initiate a calcimimetic such as cinacalcet to lower serum calcium and PTH in autonomous disease, as a bridge or alternative to surgery
Optimise mineral metabolism by controlling hyperphosphataemia and using active vitamin D judiciously, avoiding aggravation of the hypercalcaemia
Perform parathyroidectomy, subtotal or total with autotransplantation, for refractory autonomous disease as the definitive treatment
Localise abnormal glands preoperatively with neck ultrasound and sestamibi or 4D-CT scanning
Monitor closely after parathyroidectomy for hypocalcaemia and hungry-bone syndrome, replacing calcium and vitamin D
Protect the transplanted kidney and vasculature by correcting persistent hypercalcaemia that accelerates graft dysfunction and soft-tissue calcification
Manage the associated renal osteodystrophy with bone-density and skeletal surveillance
Coordinate care between nephrology or transplant medicine and endocrine surgery
